title: Cache-Control Directives
subtopics: Caching sensitive or personalized data safely
learning_outcomes: Explain how cache-control directives affects an API contract or implementation.
Apply the key ideas from max-age and freshness lifetimes to a concrete API example.
Identify one failure, security, or compatibility risk and describe how to verify it.

content.intro: This lesson focuses on cache-control directives in caching, conditional requests, and performance. You will connect max-age and freshness lifetimes to a concrete API contract decision, inspect a small example, and decide what evidence proves the behavior is correct.
content.why_it_matters: Cache-Control Directives matters because API consumers depend on predictable behavior even when clients, servers, networks, and stored data evolve independently. Applying max-age and freshness lifetimes deliberately reduces ambiguity, makes failures easier to diagnose, and gives tests a clear expectation.

content_blocks.title: Core idea
content_blocks.text: Caching and validators can reduce work and prevent stale reads or lost updates, but cache policy must protect sensitive representations. In this lesson, treat “Cache-Control Directives” as a design or implementation decision: name the expected behavior, identify its boundary, and verify it with a representative request or test.

content_blocks.title: Inspect the pattern: Cache-Control Directives
content_blocks.code:
HTTP/1.1 200 OK
ETag: "task-v7"
Cache-Control: private, max-age=0, must-revalidate
Content-Type: application/json

{"id":"task_42","title":"Review API contract"}

# Later update: If-Match: "task-v7"
content_blocks.expected_output: An ETag identifies a representation version. A conditional write can reject stale updates rather than silently overwriting a concurrent change.

content_blocks.title: Walkthrough
content_blocks.text: Start with “max-age and freshness lifetimes”; it establishes the vocabulary for this topic. Next, compare it with “no-cache , no-store , and private” and “Caching sensitive or personalized data safely”. In a real API, write down the observable behavior first, then test one normal request and one invalid or unauthorized request. Keep resource state, caller identity, and internal implementation details separate.

content_blocks.title: Professional review check
content_blocks.text: Measure before optimizing, and never cache sensitive data without a deliberate policy. The worked snippet is intentionally inspectable, not an executable hosted API. Replace example.test and placeholder identifiers with local test data only when you implement the lesson project.

content.run_instructions: Execution mode: static-validation. Validate JSON/YAML with a local linter or run the relevant HTTP request against the isolated service you implement for a project. Do not send illustrative example.test requests to a real service.
content.reset_steps: Use a disposable local database or test fixture for implementation work. Restore seed data between runs; never point exercises at production customer data or live payment endpoints.
troubleshooting: Check the exact HTTP method, path, status, header, media type, and payload before changing implementation code.
Separate a transport failure from an application validation failure, authorization denial, and dependency/database failure.
Confirm the example and its client tooling version are compatible; consult the linked standard or official guidance when behavior is ambiguous.
common_mistakes: Treating cache-control directives as an implementation detail rather than a documented behavior.
Testing only the happy path and ignoring malformed, unauthorized, conflicting, duplicate, or dependency-failure cases.
Publishing an example without checking version assumptions, sensitive-data exposure, and the expected output.
